content: 1. In most cases, injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) is not considered for use beyond initial screening. However, in certain situations, it may be appropriate to continue daily PrEP for clients who have demonstrated adherence over multiple refill cycles. 2. Across various regions, the increasing demand for PrEP services is expected to strain laboratory infrastructure, which is already insufficient in some areas. For example, some settings are still struggling to provide viral load (VL) testing for ART clients and will require improved access to nucleic acid testing (NAT) and VL testing for initiating CAB-LA. 3. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), there are ongoing challenges such as shortages of reagents, equipment breakdowns, COVID-19-related lab closures, and transportation issues, all of which hinder effective service delivery. 4. In Nepal, the stigma associated with HIV services creates a barrier for clients seeking PrEP. When PrEP is delivered through HIV or ART services, clients often avoid accessing these services due to fear of being associated with HIV, despite being eligible for PrEP based on their risk profile. 5. In LMICs, national shortages of antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) could extend to injectable formulations, further complicating service delivery. 6. In Australia, nurse-led consultations at the PrEPMe clinic at Alfred Hospital provide free services (excluding medication costs) to overseas-born individuals ineligible for Medicare. This clinic transitioned from a study-based model (PrEPX) to its current population due to high demand. 7. Over time, even bi-monthly CAB-LA visits may become burdensome for clients. There is a need for longer-acting options, such as vaccines, to improve retention in care. 8. In Poland and the UK, bi-monthly intramuscular injections and clinic visits may pose logistical challenges for clients, particularly those with busy schedules or limited access to healthcare facilities. 9. In the UK, there is confusion regarding the storage requirements for CAB-LA, despite the absence of cold-chain requirements. This highlights the need for better information and training for providers. 10. In some LMICs, providers report that refrigeration requirements for CAB-LA are a significant barrier to service delivery, especially in non-traditional settings. This may stem from confusion with CAB-RPV-LA used for treatment. 11. In Myanmar, civil unrest and COVID-19 restrictions have disrupted PrEP delivery, which is currently limited to Yangon. Clients who relocate for safety or economic reasons face challenges in maintaining adherence due to the lack of access to refills and monitoring. 12. In Lebanon, overlapping crises (economic, political, unemployment, refugee influx, and COVID-19) have destabilized the lives of PrEP users, making adherence increasingly difficult. 13. In some settings, clients may hesitate to accept new products like CAB-LA, but providers view these innovations as user-friendly and beneficial. 14. In high-volume clinics, such as those in Ukraine with 2,000 ART clients, only a small percentage of clients may be able to access injectable treatments due to logistical constraints. 15. In Thailand, providers note that attending clinic appointments for PrEP services can be time-consuming for clients, which may deter them from seeking care. 16. Barriers to CAB-LA implementation include costs (testing and clinic visits), lack of national policies, stigma, aversion to injections, civil conflicts, stockouts, and challenges in safely discontinuing CAB-LA. 17. Updated WHO guidance is needed to support advocacy, funding, and adoption of CAB-LA by health ministries. This guidance should address storage, training, counseling, administration, monitoring, and safe discontinuation. 18. In high HIV prevalence settings, sexually active individuals, especially young people with multiple partners of unknown HIV status, should be offered PrEP. 19. Some providers prioritize CAB-LA for clients at the highest risk or those with unstable life circumstances, where adherence to daily PrEP is challenging. 20. A blended approach may be necessary, allowing clients to switch between oral PrEP and injectable CAB-LA based on their needs, such as during travel or periods of increased risk. 21. In settings reliant on project funding, governments must recognize the importance of PrEP for HIV prevention to ensure sustainable service delivery. 22. Scheduling flexibility for CAB-LA administration is critical, as clients may miss follow-up appointments or require adjustments to the standard bi-monthly schedule. 23. In Australia, evening clinics are being planned to accommodate clients after work hours, but additional resources will be needed to manage the increased demand for CAB-LA. 24. In Mexico, partner NGOs providing counseling and testing may face challenges in delivering CAB-LA due to a lack of trained nurses and doctors. 25. In Zimbabwe, current PrEP providers, primarily nurses, are trained to administer injections, making CAB-LA implementation feasible with minimal additional training. 26. Task-shifting and training other cadres of healthcare workers can help meet the increased demand for CAB-LA, especially in regions like Europe, Africa, and the Western Pacific. 27. Training and refresher courses for service providers are essential to ensure proper implementation of CAB-LA, including eligibility assessment, injection administration, adherence counseling, and safe discontinuation.
